title: Fix issues with trainable_parameters_mask in MaxTextTrainingEngine
body:
# Description

When `trainable_parameters_mask` is specified, `get_optimizer()` wraps the optimizer with `optax.multi_transform` to map non-matching parameters to `optax.set_to_zero()`. While this prevents updates to frozen weights, autodiff still computes non-zero gradients for all parameters.

In `MaxTextTrainingEngine._update_kernel`, `grad_norm` and `apply_gradient_clipping` were computed over the unmasked gradients before the optimizer zeroed the updates. On models with frozen components (such as freezing router gate kernels in MoE RL training), this caused:
1. `grad_norm` to be inflated by frozen weights.
2. `apply_gradient_clipping` to aggressively over-clip trainable weights based on the inflated global norm.
3. Spikes on frozen parameters to trigger false-positive step skips when `skip_step_on_spikes` is enabled.

This change:
- Masks out frozen parameter gradients in `_update_kernel` before computing `grad_norm` and applying gradient clipping.
- Caches `_freeze_mask_fn` and `_freeze_mask` across eager and compiled execution paths in `MaxTextTrainingEngine`.
- Extracts `apply_trainable_parameters_mask` in `optimizers.py` with diagnostic logging of frozen parameter counts and sample paths.
- Adds unit tests in `maxtext_engine_test.py` covering eager and compiled execution with `trainable_parameters_mask`.

# Tests

title: DSV4: Add mhc_split_axis_contraction to contract the mHC rate and embed axes separately
body:
# Description
Adds `mhc_split_axis_contraction`, an opt-in path that keeps the mHC rate and TP-sharded embedding axes separate through RMS normalization and the fused alpha projection. The split contractions replace flatten-induced activation gathers with reductions over the sharded embedding axis.

When enabled, the checkpoint layout of the mHC parameters changes: the norm scale uses `(k, dim)` instead of `(k * dim,)`, and the alphas use `(k, dim, n)` instead of `(k * dim, n)`. Their initialized values equal the flat initialization reshaped, so converting a flag-off checkpoint is a pure reshape.

The flag defaults to false, preserving the existing RMSNorm module, parameter shapes, RNG draw order, and contraction path. DeepSeek-V4 Hugging Face conversion reshapes alpha weights for either layout, and Muon contracts both split input axes.

# Performance
Step time was 7.711 s/step with `mhc_split_axis_contraction` disabled and 6.811 s/step with it enabled, a 1.13x result.

Reproduction setup: v6e-128, DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B, LoRA fine-tuning, `ici_expert_parallelism=16`, `ici_tensor_parallelism=8`, `ici_fsdp_parallelism=1`, `max_target_length=16384`, `per_device_batch_size=0.125` (global batch 16), `LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS=--xla_tpu_scoped_vmem_limit_kib=98304`, dynamic-splash attention path enabled, with `mhc_split_axis_contraction` toggled.

# Tests
- `JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu pytest -q tests/unit/mhc_test.py -k split_axis` — 3 passed; the split path matches Sinkhorn and mHC-lite outputs, and its initialized parameters are exact reshapes of the flat layout.
- `JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu pytest -q tests/unit/mhc_test.py` — 27 passed, 2 skipped.
- `JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu pytest -q tests/unit/param_mapping_test.py tests/unit/muon_utils_test.py` — 53 passed; split-layout Hugging Face conversion round-trips and Muon uses the intended contraction axes.

title: Keep nnx.RngState when writing scanned and rematerialized decoder state back.
body:
Keep nnx.RngState when writing scanned and rematerialized decoder state back.

An `nnx.Rngs` stream draws `fold_in(key, count)` and then increments `count`. The key never changes, so `count` is the only thing that makes two successive draws differ, and it has to survive the round trip through any JAX transform. `NNXDecoder._apply_layers_sequentially` filtered `nnx.RngState` out of the state it wrote back after `jax.lax.scan`, and `_apply_remainder_block` popped it out of the state returned from `jax.checkpoint`. Both discard the counter increments, so the layer stack rewinds its RNG streams to their pre-transform values on every call and replays the identical dropout mask on every training step.

The failure is silent: no shape change, no error. It is also invisible to tooling — `jax_debug_key_reuse` only inspects typed keys and models `fold_in` as a pure source, and no linter can see a counter that was dropped rather than misused. It is latent at HEAD because `dropout_rate` defaults to `0.0`, and at rate 0 `linears.Dropout` sets `self.rngs = None` so there is no RNG state for the filters to drop — but `scan_layers` defaults to true, so any run that turns dropout on hits it immediately.

`tests/unit/nnx_rng_state_test.py` reproduces it: build an `NNXDecoder` at `dropout_rate=0.1`, record every `nnx.RngCount`, run one forward pass, and assert the dropout-stream counters increased. `test_scanned_layers_dropout_counts_advance` and `test_remainder_block_dropout_counts_advance` both fail before this change and pass after. `test_unscanned_layers_dropout_counts_advance` exercises the non-scanned path, which already threads the state correctly, and passes both before and after — so the assertion is not merely over-strict. Only the `dropout` stream is asserted on; the `params` stream and a module's own stored `self.rngs` are drawn at construction time and correctly do not move during a forward pass.

Writing the full scanned state back, and popping only `nnx.Intermediate` from the rematerialized block, lets the incremented counters leave the transform and land back in the module, so the next call folds in a different count and draws a different mask. Intermediates are still dropped from the rematerialized block: returning them would keep the sown activations alive as residuals, which is what the remat is there to avoid.

The state round-trips without any shape or sharding change. `nnx_scan.create_scanned_layers` forks the stream with `split=length` and Flax sizes the counter to match the key, so both enter the scan stacked as `(length,)` and come back out the same. Two sibling call sites already do the unfiltered thing and are the model for this change: `nnx_scan.apply_scanned_layers` writes the full state back including `nnx.RngState`, and `_apply_layer_with_remat` returns the whole `nnx.state` out of `jax.checkpoint`. Inference is unaffected, since at `dropout_rate=0` there is no `nnx.RngState` and the filters were no-ops.

The three `tests/utils/reference_hlo_*.txt` goldens are regenerated because this change alters the emitted HLO. `tests/integration/hlo_diff_test.py` compares a freshly compiled module against a checked-in reference, and threading `nnx.RngState` out of `jax.lax.scan` widens the scan carry, so the references no longer match. The diff is large (1014 lines across the three files) but almost entirely mechanical: after normalizing away XLA's instruction-name suffixes only 112 lines differ, and those are the new `u32` `copy-start`/`copy-done` pairs for the RNG key and counter now living in the carry, plus the tuple-index shift in `%wide.param` that widening the carry forces on every later member. That the goldens move at all is the HLO-level confirmation of the bug: before this change the RNG state was not in the carry, which is exactly why the counters could not survive the scan.

These were not regenerated by hand. They come from the `Update HLO References` GitHub workflow run on the exported branch (`tests/utils/update_hlo_references.py` under the pinned CI container, `--resolution=lowest`, `LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS=--xla_tpu_scoped_vmem_limit_kib=65536`), which is the only environment the goldens are valid against -- the reference text embeds memory-space annotations that depend on libtpu's VMEM budget, so a locally produced file would not match CI even when the code is identical. The pre-regeneration goldens on the exported branch were verified byte-identical to the ones in google3 before the new files were copied back, so this diff is exactly what CI produced and nothing else.

title: Advance the PRNG key between inference steps instead of reusing a single key.
body:
Advance the PRNG key between inference steps instead of reusing a single key.

`InferenceWorker.rng` and `PrefillHelper.rng` default to `jax.random.PRNGKey(0)` and were never advanced, so the autoregressive decode loop handed an identical key to every `generate` call and every prompt was prefilled with the same key. The same single key was also shared between `MaxEngine.load_params`, the prefill helper, and `init_decode_state`; and in `prefill_concat` every prompt in a packed batch sampled its first token from one key. For any non-greedy `decode_sampling_strategy` this removes the independence that weighted and top-k sampling assume: successive tokens and parallel requests are drawn from a single key and end up deterministically correlated. This is the defect fixed upstream in AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext PR #946, reintroduced by code written after that fix landed.

MLPerf hits a second, distinct mechanism. `MaxEngine.aot_compile` has a `pass_rng_shape` switch, and with `pass_rng_shape=False` the *public*, stateful `generate` method is traced. The `self.rng, rng = jax.random.split(self.rng)` inside it therefore runs once, at trace time, and the resulting concrete key is constant-folded into the compiled executable. Every later invocation replays that one key regardless of what the caller passes.

Two latent footguns are closed as well. `MaxEngine.load_params` and `init_decode_state` have signatures of the form `(self, *args, rng=None, **kwargs)`, so a key passed positionally is swallowed by `*args` and silently replaced by `PRNGKey(0)` — which is exactly what the `offline_engine.py` call site did. `BatchedPrefillProcessor` had no key of its own at all.

The fix keeps key advancement in eager Python, outside any trace, and passes the key in as a compiled input: split before each decode step, each prefill, and each prefill bucket; derive independent keys for the engine, the prefill helper, and the decode state; `fold_in(rng, idx)` per packed prompt; and flip MLPerf to `pass_rng_shape=True` so the key becomes an input slot in the graph rather than a constant. Turning the key into an argument does not trigger recompilation, because a jit cache key is (function, static args, input shape/dtype) and `uint32[2]` is invariant. No `rng=None` default is removed, so no external caller signature changes.

`test_prng_keys_advance_during_inference` in `tests/unit/offline_engine_test.py` reproduces the core bug: it snapshots `InferenceWorker.rng` and `PrefillHelper.rng`, runs one `batch_inference`, and asserts both advanced. Before this change neither moves and the test fails deterministically. The stored keys are asserted on rather than the sampled tokens because a stale key changes how successive draws are correlated, not necessarily their values, so comparing completions would not reliably detect it. All three tests in `offline_engine_test.py` pass with this change; reverting just the two `jax.random.split` calls makes the new test fail with "the decode loop did not advance its PRNG key". 

A second unrelated fix rides along in `offline_engine.py`. The detokenization thread did `int(first_token)` and `int(result_tokens_at_slot)` on numpy arrays of shape `(1,)`. NumPy has been tightening this for years: silently accepted before 1.25, `DeprecationWarning` from 1.25 through 2.3, and a hard `TypeError: only 0-dimensional arrays can be converted to Python scalars` from 2.4 onward. `pyproject.toml` pins `numpy>=2.1.3` with no upper bound, so any environment resolving to 2.4+ crashes the detokenization thread on every `batch_inference` call, not just under test. Both sites now use `.item()`, which is exactly what old NumPy did implicitly for size-1 arrays and still raises for larger ones. This was found because it is what blocked the new test from running at all.

One more unrelated fix rides along in `prefill_packing.py`, because the same call site had to change anyway to thread the key through `in_shardings` and `.lower()`. The AOT branch of `_process_bucket` passed `return_prompt_logp` to the compiled callable, but that argument is declared as a `static_argname`. An AOT-compiled function accepts only its non-static arguments, so that branch raised `TypeError: Function compiled with input pytree does not match the input pytree it was called with` on every invocation. The argument is dropped from the compiled call.

A third rides-along fix, in the same function. `_process_batch_compiled` tested its ahead-of-time compilation cache with a 2-tuple, `(padded_length, num_prompts)`, but stored and returned the entry under a 3-tuple that also includes `return_prompt_logp`. The membership test therefore never matched, and `jax.jit(...).lower(...).compile()` re-ran on every call instead of once per bucket, defeating the purpose of the AOT path. The lookup and the insertion now share one `cache_key`. This defect predates the change -- `g4 annotate` attributes those lines to cl/869967557, the import of GitHub PR #3124 -- and is fixed here only because this CL already had to edit that function.

title: Plumb tunix reward_num_workers into the RL trainer with a picklable reward wrapper
body:
## What

Split out of #5236 per review. Forwards `GrpoConfig.reward_num_workers` / `reward_worker_timeout_seconds` (process-pool evaluation of the reward functions) from the MaxText RL config to both the standard and the agentic learner, filtered through `_kwargs_supported_by` so an older pinned tunix keeps working.

**The plumbing alone would be a no-op**, which is why this is a separate PR: `make_reward_fn` wrapped every reward fn in a nested closure, which cannot be pickled into tunix's reward worker pool — the first call raises `PicklingError` inside the pool and tunix silently falls back to serial parent-process evaluation forever (log signature: `Reward fn ... failed in worker processes (PicklingError...)`). This PR replaces the closure with `_RewardFn`, a module-level callable class that pickles by reference to the underlying reward fn plus the config, so the pool actually engages.

**`check_numbers` is not parallelized by this knob.** Of the three built-in reward fns only `match_format_exactly` and `match_format_approximately` run in the workers. `check_numbers` grades through `math_verify_pool`, which builds its own process pool; pool workers are daemonic and may not have children, so inside a reward worker it raises `AssertionError: daemonic processes are not allowed to have children`. tunix catches that, adds `check_numbers` to its parent-only set and evaluates it in the parent for the rest of the run. The fallback is immediate (an assertion, not a timeout), and `math_verify_pool` still parallelizes the expensive `math_verify` grading from the parent; only `extract_answer` / `preprocess_math_string` / the string comparisons stay serial (#5235 made `extract_answer` 4.8x faster). So with the default reward stack, expect a smaller speedup than the worker count suggests. Making `check_numbers` parallelize needs `math_verify_pool` to detect that it is already inside a worker and grade inline — a separate change. A test pins the current behavior.

Custom reward functions loaded from a user file (`reward_functions_path`) are covered too. tunix starts its workers from a fork server, so they are fresh interpreters that do not inherit the parent's `sys.modules` and have to import the user module by name. `load_custom_callable` gains an opt-in `importable_by_workers` mode, used for reward fns only: the file is loaded under its own module name (`/path/my_rewards.py` -> `my_rewards`), registered in `sys.modules`, and its directory is appended to `sys.path` (multiprocessing hands `sys.path` to the workers). That only happens when it cannot shadow anything — the file name must be a valid identifier and no *other* module of that name may be loaded or importable (a name that resolves to the file itself, e.g. when the file sits in the launch cwd that `python -m` puts on `sys.path`, is not a conflict) — and several fns from one file share one module object. Otherwise, and for every other caller (`process_data`), the file is loaded privately exactly as before; such a callable fails to pickle in the parent, so tunix falls back to the parent immediately instead of losing a worker and waiting out `reward_worker_timeout_seconds`. The existing `load_custom_callable` contract tests (no `sys.path` change, no basename in `sys.modules`) are untouched.

## Effect

Serial reward scoring of 2048 completions costs ~30 s/step on a Qwen3-0.6B GRPO run. How much of that a run recovers depends on its reward stack: fns that run in the workers scale with `reward_num_workers`, while `check_numbers` keeps its own `math_verify_pool` parallelism in the parent (see above).

## Tests

`tests/post_training/unit/train_rl_test.py`:
- the new fields default to tunix's defaults and accept overrides (also declared in `configs/post_train/rl.yml`);
- `_RewardFn` pickle round-trips and preserves `__name__` / the bound config — with the production pydantic `RLConfig`, not just a stub;
- a reward file whose directory is already on `sys.path` (the launch-from-cwd case) still loads under its own name and runs in a fork-server worker;
- two reward fns loaded from one user file run in a real fork-server worker (an in-process pickle round trip cannot catch a module name the worker is unable to import);
- a user file named like an existing module (`json.py`) loads privately, leaves that module and `sys.path` alone, and fails to pickle in the parent (the immediate-fallback path);
- `check_numbers` next to a worker-friendly fn: only `check_numbers` lands in tunix's parent-only set, the fallback does not wait for the worker timeout, and the scores are correct;
- an integration test builds a real tunix `SequenceRewardManager` with `reward_num_workers=2` and asserts the parent-only fallback set stays **empty** after a batch — i.e. the pool really evaluated the wrapper (skips when the installed tunix predates the knob).

```
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest tests/post_training/unit/train_rl_test.py -k "reward_worker or reward_fn or custom or check_numbers"
```

## Notes

Builds on #5236 (merged; reuses its `_kwargs_supported_by` helper). Rebased onto main, so the diff is the reward-only change.

- [x] I have added tests that prove the change works.
- [x] Defaults leave existing configs untouched.

title: Pin reference matmul precision to HIGHEST in csa_streamindex TPU parity tests
body:
# Description

Two `csa_streamindex` TPU tests fail on TPU7x (`test_parallel_dimension_semantics_accepted`,
`test_shard_map_multi_device_parity`), both with ~0.03% of elements off by up to 0.057.
They pass on v6e.

The kernel is fine — the reference is the imprecise side. `csa_indexer_scores_jax` contracts
over heads at the default precision, which on TPU7x lowers to a single-pass bf16 MXU matmul.
That rounds the f32 per-head scores to bf16 before summing 16 heads, and wherever that sum
cancels the leftover absolute error lands on a near-zero result, so `atol=2e-2` fails.
The Pallas kernel accumulates in f32 throughout.

Fix is to pin the reference to `Precision.HIGHEST` in both assertions so they measure the
kernel rather than the reference's lowering. Tolerances are unchanged — agreement is now
~1e-5, so there is plenty of margin.

# Tests

Existing tests; this only changes how they compute `expected`. Modeled both contraction
precisions offline and the bf16 version reproduces the CI signature (0.024% violations,
max abs 0.036, max rel 2.1 vs CI's 0.028% / 0.057 / 4.2), which is what identifies the
reference as the side at fault.

Note: I could not run TPU7x locally, so the fix rests on that analysis rather than a
hardware repro — CI on this PR is the real check.

### Description
This PR enables cleanly overriding the GMM tile sizes for both the forward and backward passes of Tokamax (`ragged_dot`) in MaxText using an elegant global heuristics monkey-patching approach.

**Proposed Changes**

* **Heuristics Monkey-Patching (`src/maxtext/layers/moe.py`)**: Instead of introducing complex custom `vjp` function wrappers or polluting model layers with low-level compilation code, this PR dynamically monkey-patches `PallasMosaicTpuRaggedDot._get_heuristics_config` globally during RoutedMoE initialization.
* **Dynamic Shapes & Pass Routing**: The monkey-patch dynamically inspects the shapes of the operands (`lhs`/`rhs`) and the JAX dimension numbers. This allows it to detect the active pass (**Forward**, **Backward DLHS**, or **Backward DRHS**) and layer type (**Weight Input `wi`** or **Weight Output `wo`**) on the fly, applying your exact manual tile configurations:

title: [ROCm] optimizations to reduce temp size prior to training starts
body:
# Description

The purpose of this PR is to reduce temp (compile) memory consumption. The optimizations have been tested on ROCm (MI355) and CUDA (H100), from which temp size was reduced. However, we would like to see your help for testing them on TPU to check if they are applicable or not. 

 ## Checklist
  - [x] Code follows the project style guidelines (pyink formatting applied)

The PR might be a bit big, however, we can split into several PRs, if that helps to review them on your side. 

| Configuration | PP | EP | Temp (main) | Temp (cj/tmem-fixes-clean) | Reduction |
|---------------|----|----|------------:|------------------:|----------:|
| ds-proxy-se2-e256-h4096 | 8 | 1 | 36.5 GB | 20.4 GB | **−16.1 GB (−44%)** |
| ds-proxy-N1-ep2-pp4     | 4 | 2 | 44.4 GB | 22.9 GB | **−21.5 GB (−48%)** |

We also detail the files changed along with the reason behind them.

## 1. `src/maxtext/configs/base.yml` -- Default `float32_weight_sum` to false

**What changed:** `float32_weight_sum: true` --> `false`

**Why:** When MoE models sum expert weights, using fp32 precision requires promoting all expert weight tensors to float32, then summing, then casting back. This materializes ~2 GB of temporary f32 tensors per device. By defaulting to false, we keep the summation in the model's native dtype (bf16), which avoids the temporary buffers entirely.

**Trade-off:** Slightly reduced numerical precision in expert weight summation. For bf16 training this is unlikely to matter in practice, and the parameter remains configurable for users who need strict fp32 summation.

---

## 2. `src/maxtext/configs/types.py` -- Pydantic field default alignment

**What changed:** `float32_weight_sum` field default `True` --> `False`, description updated.

**Why:** Mirrors the base.yml change so the Pydantic config schema and the YAML config file agree on the default.

---

## 3. `src/maxtext/kernels/gather_reduce_sc.py` -- JIT decorator restructuring

**What changed:** `@jax.jit(static_argnames=[...])` --> `@functools.partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=[...])`

**Why:** The direct `@jax.jit(...)` decorator form can interact poorly with certain JAX versions when the decorated function is further wrapped or inspected. `functools.partial` preserves function metadata (name, docstring) and ensures the decorator is properly composed. This is a robustness fix that prevents subtle compilation issues.

---

## 4. `src/maxtext/utils/sharding.py` -- `skip_trivial_specs` + `remove_size_one_mesh_axis`

**What changed:** Two additions:

**(a) `skip_trivial_specs` parameter on `maybe_shard_with_logical()`:**
When `skip_trivial_specs=True`, the function checks if all axes in the sharding spec resolve to `None` or `()`. If so, it returns the input tensor unchanged -- no `with_sharding_constraint` call is emitted. This is the foundational optimization used by attentions.py, pipeline.py, and mixtral.py.

**Why:** `jax.lax.with_sharding_constraint` is not free even when the spec is trivial. XLA can materialize copy buffers to enforce a constraint that effectively does nothing. Skipping it when the spec is all-None avoids those temporaries.

**(b) `remove_size_one_mesh_axis()` function:**
Filters out mesh axes from a `PartitionSpec` where the corresponding mesh dimension has size 1. For example, on a single-node setup where `stage=1`, any sharding over `"stage"` is meaningless and can be dropped.

**Why:** Size-1 mesh axes create sharding overhead (XLA inserts identity reshards) without providing any actual parallelism. Removing them simplifies the HLO and eliminates associated temporary buffers. The existing `logical_to_mesh_axes()` was refactored to call this new function automatically.

---

## 5. `src/maxtext/layers/normalizations.py` -- Replace einsum with multiply in RMSNorm

**What changed:**
- `jnp.einsum("...k,k->...k", y, effective_scale, out_sharding=...)` --> `y * effective_scale` + separate `jax.lax.with_sharding_constraint`
- Added conditional: `effective_scale = scale + self.scale_offset if self.scale_offset != 0.0 else scale`

**Why:** The `einsum("...k,k->...k", ...)` operation is semantically just element-wise multiplication (broadcasting the 1D scale across the leading dims). However, XLA's einsum lowering can generate larger intermediate buffers than a direct multiply, especially inside `lax.scan` (pipeline parallelism). Inside a scan body, these intermediates get hoisted into the scan carry by XLA's `loop_broadcast_fusion` pass, permanently increasing the carry size.

By using direct multiplication, XLA generates a simpler `broadcast + multiply` HLO sequence with no intermediate allocation. The sharding constraint is decoupled and applied only when needed (`out_sharding is not None`).

The `scale_offset != 0.0` check avoids a pointless addition when offset is zero (the standard RMSNorm case, vs. RMSNorm with learnable offset).

---

## 6. `src/maxtext/layers/attentions.py` -- `skip_trivial_specs=True`

**What changed:** Added `skip_trivial_specs=True` to `maybe_shard_with_logical()` call in the Attention class.

**Why:** On mesh configurations where the attention output sharding resolves to all-None (e.g., no tensor parallelism), this avoids materializing a copy buffer. This is a minor but consistent optimization applied across the codebase.

---

## 7. `src/maxtext/layers/embeddings.py` -- 2 GB iota_embed guard + sharding constraints

**What changed:**
- **Iota guard:** Compute one-hot tensor size as `batch * seq * vocab * dtype_size`. If >2 GB, fall back to gather-based embedding instead of iota (one-hot) embedding.
- **Conditional sharding:** Only create `out_pspec`/`out_sharding` when `shard_mode == ShardMode.EXPLICIT`.
- **Logical constraints:** Added `nn.with_logical_constraint(output, ...)` after the embedding lookup.

**Why:** Iota embedding works by creating a one-hot matrix of shape `[batch, seq, vocab]` and multiplying by the embedding table. For large vocabularies (e.g., vocab=102400), this one-hot tensor can be enormous: `8 * 4096 * 102400 * 2 bytes = 6.7 GB` in bf16. XLA materializes this entire tensor even though only one element per row is non-zero. The gather-based path (`jnp.take`) uses constant memory regardless of vocabulary size.

The 2 GB threshold is conservative -- it covers most common model configs while still allowing small-vocab models to use the faster iota path.

The sharding spec was being computed unconditionally even when `shard_mode != EXPLICIT`. Moving it under a conditional avoids unnecessary mesh lookups.

---

## 8. `src/maxtext/layers/attention_op.py` -- Causal mask for synthetic data

**What changed:** For `dataset_type == "synthetic"`, skip materializing the attention mask tensors entirely. Use `mask_type="causal"` directly instead of computing mask arrays.

**Why:** With synthetic data, segment IDs are always all-ones (a single segment per sequence). The segment mask is therefore all-True, so the combined attention mask reduces to pure causal masking. By using `mask_type="causal"` natively, we avoid:
1. Materializing `f32/s32[batch, 1, seq, seq]` mask tensors (~5 GiB for seq=4096, batch=8)
2. These masks being hoisted into the scan carry by XLA's `loop_broadcast_fusion` pass

Also removed two dead parameters from the `DotProductAttention` call:
- `scale_factor=1.0` (no-op: default is already 1.0)
- `context_parallel_strategy=...` (not used in this non-CP code path)

---

## 9. `src/maxtext/layers/moe.py` -- Tile truncation + remove redundant astype

**What changed:**
**(a) Tile size tuples:** Reduced from 9-tuples to 3-tuples (forward-only).

**(b) Removed `.astype(self.dtype)`** from `return intermediate_layer`.

**Why (a):** The 9-tuple `wi_tile_size` and `wo_tile_size` contain tiling parameters for forward (fwd), dlhs (backward LHS), and drhs (backward RHS) passes of the Group Matrix Multiply (GMM). When `megablox=False` (the JAX `ragged_dot` path), only the forward pass tile values are used -- the backward-pass tile values are allocated in the tuple but never read. By truncating to 3-tuples, we avoid allocating and passing unused tile parameters.

**Why (b):** The `intermediate_layer` is already computed in the correct dtype from the matmul operations. The explicit `.astype(self.dtype)` creates a redundant copy that XLA cannot always elide (especially inside scan bodies). Removing it avoids one tensor-sized temporary.

---

## 10. `src/maxtext/layers/pipeline.py` -- Replace ppermute with slice/concat, reduce remat

**What changed:** Multiple optimizations in the `Pipeline` class (not `CircularPipeline`):

**(a) Replace `shard_map+ppermute` with `lax.slice`/`jnp.concatenate`/`jnp.pad`:**

The old `_rotate_right` used `@jax.shard_map` with `jax.lax.ppermute` for circular shifting across pipeline stages. The new version uses `lax.slice_in_dim` + `jnp.concatenate`:
```python
last = lax.slice_in_dim(arr, N-1, N, axis=0)
rest = lax.slice_in_dim(arr, 0, N-1, axis=0)
return jnp.concatenate([last, rest], axis=0)
```

The old `_shift_right` used `ppermute` + zero-fill. The new version uses `jnp.pad` + `lax.slice`:
```python
padded = jnp.pad(arr, [[1,0]] + [[0,0]]*(ndim-1))
return lax.slice(padded, [0]*ndim, arr.shape)
```

Similarly, `_update_state_io` was converted from `shard_map`+`ppermute`-based left-shift to `pad`+`slice_in_dim`-based left-shift.

**Why:** XLA's `loop_broadcast_fusion` pass hoists ppermute's collective communication buffers into the scan carry. For `pp=4`, this added **10-15 GB** of temporary memory. Slice-based operations don't use collective scratch space -- they operate on local arrays. The operations are mathematically identical (they perform the same circular/linear shift) but have very different memory footprints inside scan loops.

**(b) Remove unnecessary sharding constraints:**
- Removed sharding on `shift`, `first_stage_in`, `microbatches_processed` -- these are small tensors where sharding adds overhead without benefit.
- Removed `out_sharding` from `broadcasted_iota` call.
- Added `skip_trivial_specs=True` to the base sharding helper.

**(c) Remove `decoder_layer_input` from remat save list:**
Changed from `save_only_these_names("iteration_input", "decoder_layer_input")` to `save_only_these_names("iteration_input")`. The `iteration_input` checkpoint already contains the data needed for backward pass. Saving `decoder_layer_input` too created two redundant stacked checkpoint buffers (~3.3 GB).

**(d) Remove `meta.remove_axis` call:**
The axis removal logic for vmap weights was unnecessary and created intermediate metadata objects.

**(e) Replace indexed gather with `dynamic_slice_in_dim`:**
`x.at[idx].get(out_sharding=...)` creates intermediate index tuples. `jax.lax.dynamic_slice_in_dim(x, i, 1, dim)` is a single primitive with no intermediate allocation.

---

## 11. `src/maxtext/models/deepseek.py` -- Remove reshard calls

**What changed:**
- Added import: `from maxtext.utils.sharding import remove_size_one_mesh_axis`
- Changed MoE kernel init scale from `self.config.dense_init_scale` to `1.0`
- Replaced explicit `jax.reshard()` in/out pair with `remove_size_one_mesh_axis()`-based PartitionSpec
- Expanded PartitionSpec to include `"fsdp_transpose"` and `"context"` axes

**Why:** The original code captured the input sharding, resharded inputs to a specific activation PartitionSpec, ran the MoE block, then resharded outputs back to the original input sharding. Each `jax.reshard()` creates a full-activation-sized temporary buffer. By using `remove_size_one_mesh_axis()` to simplify the PartitionSpec (dropping axes that have size 1 on the current mesh), we get the same effective sharding without the explicit reshard calls. This eliminates two activation-sized temporaries.

The PartitionSpec was also expanded to include `fsdp_transpose` and `context` axes for correctness on meshes that use those dimensions.

---

## 12. `src/maxtext/models/mixtral.py` -- NNX to Linen conversion

**What changed:** Complete rewrite from `nnx.Module` to `nn.Module` (Linen).

- Removed `from flax import nnx` and `nnx_wrappers` imports
- Added `attention_as_linen`, `rms_norm`, `maybe_shard_with_logical` imports
- Changed class from `nnx.Module` (with `__init__`) to `nn.Module` (with `@nn.compact` `__call__`)
- All layer instantiation moved from `__init__` into `__call__`
- Added local `shard()` helper with `skip_trivial_specs=True`
- Removed `MixtralDecoderLayerToLinen = nnx_wrappers.to_linen_class(...)` wrapper -- the class IS Linen now

**Why:** The NNX-to-Linen wrapper (`nnx_wrappers.to_linen_class`) creates an NNX module graph and then converts it to Linen form. This process materializes intermediate module objects and parameter trees that consume memory during `eval_shape` and `jit` tracing. By writing the layer directly in Linen, we bypass this overhead entirely.

The Linen `@nn.compact` style also defers all parameter creation to call time, avoiding eager allocation of layer parameters during module construction. This is particularly impactful for MoE models where the number of parameters is large.

Weight names are preserved through explicit `name=` arguments to ensure checkpoint compatibility.

---

## 13. `src/maxtext/trainers/pre_train/train.py` -- Flax config + grad dtype guard

**What changed:**
**(a)** Added `import flax` + `flax.config.update("flax_always_shard_variable", False)` at module level, guarded by `try/except LookupError`.

**(b)** Wrapped the gradient dtype tree_map in `if config.grad_dtype != jnp.float32:`.

**Why (a):** When `flax_always_shard_variable` is True (the default in some Flax versions), Flax inserts `with_sharding_constraint` on every variable during creation. This generates intermediate sharding copies even for variables that don't need explicit sharding. Setting it to False means sharding is only applied where the model code explicitly requests it.

**Why (b):** The tree_map that casts gradients from fp32 to `config.grad_dtype` is a no-op when `grad_dtype` is already fp32. But `tree_map` still walks the entire gradient tree and calls the lambda on every leaf, which can trigger unnecessary tensor copies if XLA doesn't fully elide the identity cast. Skipping the tree_map entirely when it's a no-op avoids this overhead.

title: [NNX] NNX migration (12/N): delete Linen code paths, classes, and NNX compatibility flags
body:
## NNX Migration Route Map
1. ✅ Add NNX scaffolding: `pure_nnx` flag, `init_state_fn`, `TrainStateNNX`, NNX utils. Linen workflow unchanged. (PR #3427)
2. ✅ NNX sharding utilities: `get_abstract_state_nnx`, `get_named_sharding_nnx`, `set_named_sharding_nnx`, `get_partition_spec_nnx`, `get_mesh_from_config`. (PR #3470)
3. ✅ NNX fully supported end-to-end: `TrainStateNNX`, model creation, gradient accumulation, checkpointing, and training loop dispatch. (PR #3500)
4. ✅ Sharding diagnostics on NNX, plus post-training bugfixes that surfaced once the NNX path got exercised end-to-end. (PR #3652)
5. ✅ NNX correctness fixes, feature enablements, and vocab tiling on NNX.
6. ✅ NNX-native DPO.
7. ✅ NNX-native MaxEngine inference. (PR #3821)
8. ✅ NNX-native LoRA + GRPO. (PR #3824)
9. ✅ NNX-aware QK-Clip + remaining checkpoint utilities. (PR #3836)
9.5. ✅ NNX + AQT in MaxEngine + serve-mode reload + gpt3 prefill fix. (PR #3844)
10. ✅ Vocab tiling `custom_vjp` for NNX (+ output-head carve-out).
11. ✅ Flip NNX defaults to `True`. (#3526)
12. 🔄 **[This PR]** Delete the Linen code paths, classes/helpers, and the `pure_nnx` / `enable_nnx` / `pure_nnx_decoder` flags. (#4038)

## Description

PR11 made NNX the default and PR6–PR10 promoted every routed-to-Linen feature to NNX-native, so NNX is the only production path. This PR **deletes Linen**: all flag/`isinstance` dispatch, the dead Linen classes and `*_as_linen` wrappers, the three compatibility flags, and the now-obsolete Linen-only tests.

**Net: 64 files, +728 / −6,205 (−5,477 lines).** Organized into 4 reviewable commits (ordered so each is self-consistent — flags removed last, after every reference is gone):

| Commit | Files | What |
|---|---|---|
| **1/4** collapse dispatch | 19 | Statically simplify every `pure_nnx` / `enable_nnx` / `isinstance(model, nn.Module)` branch to the NNX path across core training / utils / inference / RL / checkpoint-conversion. Zero executable flag reads remain in src. |
| **2/4** delete Linen classes | 13 | Delete `TransformerLinenPure`; the Linen `Decoder` / `DecoderLayer` / `SequentialBlockDecoderLayers` stack (`decoders.py` 1525→47, only `deepstack_process` kept); and **28 dead `*_as_linen` ToLinen wrappers** across the layer/model files. The wrapped NNX classes are untouched. |
| **3/4** test cleanup | 25 | Delete obsolete Linen-only tests, drop redundant flag args from the rest, and fix `hlo_diff_test` (see below). |
| **4/4** remove flags | 7 | Remove the three flags from `types.py`, `base.yml`, `inference/vllm.yml`, `pyconfig`, and the post-train distillation configs. |



## Stats

**Diff: 64 files, +728 / −6,205 (net −5,477), in 4 commits** — overwhelmingly deletion (it's a "remove dead Linen" PR). Production-vs-test split:

| Area | Files | Insertions | Deletions | Net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Production code** (`src/maxtext`) | 39 | +520 | −4,662 | −4,142 |
|   • core / training / utils / inference / RL | 19 | +474 | −1,896 | −1,422 |
|   • layers + models (Linen classes / `*_as_linen`) | 13 | +44 | −2,746 | −2,702 |
|   • configs (flag removal) | 7 | +2 | −20 | −18 |
| **Tests** (`tests/`) | 25 | +208 | −1,543 | −1,335 |
|   • unit | 13 | +101 | −1,261 | −1,160 |
|   • integration | 9 | +81 | −225 | −144 |
|   • test utils / assets | 3 | +26 | −57 | −31 |

So **~75% of the line changes are production code and ~25% are tests** (by deletions, 4,662 vs 1,543 ≈ 3:1). The largest single chunk is the Linen decoder stack + `*_as_linen` wrappers (−2,746 in layers/models). Note this is pure refactor/removal — **no new feature code**; the "+728" insertions are almost entirely de-indenting kept NNX branches and rewriting a handful of tests.

title: Restore needs_layout_passes=False on the SC ragged_gather_reduce v2 kernel (fixes TPU unit tests on main)
body:
## What

Restores `needs_layout_passes=False` in the `pltpu.CompilerParams` of the SparseCore `ragged_gather_reduce` v2 kernel
(`src/maxtext/kernels/ragged/ragged_gather_reduce_v2.py`). This is a one-line revert of 3e76c2a9a (#5265, "[Pallas][SC] Lower
plsc.bitcast to tpu.bitcast when layout passes are enabled"). After this change the file is byte-identical to its state before
that commit.

## Why

Since 3e76c2a9a, main's scheduled CI and every PR that runs the TPU suites fail the same jobs: **TPU Pathways Unit Tests (1, 2)**
and **TPU Pretrain Tests (tpu-unit) (1–3)**. Because `All Required Tests Passed` depends on them, unrelated PRs are blocked
from merging.

The failure, from the CI logs:

```
jax._src.pallas.mosaic.error_handling.MosaicError: INTERNAL: Operation not supported in the Mosaic-SC
infer-vector-layout pass. Set needs_layout_passes=False in the TPU custom call.

The MLIR operation involved:
  %376 = "vector.bitcast"(%375) : (vector<8xi32>) -> vector<8xf32>
```

Failing tests: the ragged-sort MoE tests in `tests/unit/moe_test.py` (for example
`RoutedMoeTest::test_ragged_sort_loss_and_grad_ring_of_experts`), `tests/unit/router_replay_test.py`
(`RaggedSortForcedRoutingEquivalenceTest`) and `tests/equiv_chunk_test.py::EquivChunkTest::test_chunk_equivalence`. One
tpu-unit shard exits with code 139 at the same test. All tracebacks go through the `pl.kernel(...)` call in
`ragged_gather_reduce_v2.py` via `layers/moe.py`.

## How it was narrowed down

- A PR run merged onto main at `a5c4c45bb` passed every suite; the next run of the same PR, merged onto `3e76c2a9a`, failed
  the jobs above. `git log a5c4c45bb..3e76c2a9a` contains exactly one commit, 3e76c2a9a, and the PR itself only changed RL
  reward-loader code in between.
- Scheduled runs on main: the run on `d49a5c029` does not have these failures; the runs on `3e76c2a9a` and `48521f17b` do.
- An unrelated PR branch tested on a base that contains 3e76c2a9a fails the same five jobs with the same error text.
- The error message itself asks for the flag this commit removed.

The likely cause is a toolchain skew: the commit expects the compiler to lower `vector.bitcast` under the layout passes, and
the JAX build that CI installs does not do that yet. The flag can be removed again once it does.

## Notes

- 3e76c2a9a was imported by copybara (`PiperOrigin-RevId: 983449116`), so the corresponding internal change may need the same
  revert, or the next sync could reintroduce the removal.
- #5251 proposes the same flag removal for the v1 kernel (`ragged_gather_reduce.py`). It will most likely hit the same error
  until the toolchain supports it.

## Tests

No local TPU run was possible; this PR's own CI is the verification. Expected result: TPU Pathways Unit Tests and TPU Pretrain
tpu-unit return to green.

## Checklist

- [x] I have performed a self-review of my code.
- [x] The change is a pure revert of a single line; no new behavior is introduced.
- [x] Defaults leave existing configs untouched.

title: Fix pipeline_utils mutating axes_to_remove and add unit tests
body:
# Description

Fixes `remove_gathered_mesh_axes` in `utils/pipeline_utils.py` mutating its `axes_to_remove` argument, and adds the first direct unit tests for `pipeline_utils`.

**The bug.** For every non-MoE leaf, `remove_gathered_mesh_axes` did `axes_to_remove.append("expert")` on the caller's list. `derive_stage_weight_partition_specs` (called from `NNXCircularPipeline.from_repeat_weights_to_bsw`) passes that same list to every leaf, so once any non-MoE leaf has been visited, `"expert"` is also stripped from the routed MoE block (`MoeBlock_0`) of every leaf visited afterwards. That contradicts the docstring ("The 'expert' mesh axis is only retained for the routed block").

**When it shows up.** JAX flattens dicts in sorted key order. In a single decoder layer `MoeBlock_0` sorts before its lowercase siblings (`self_attention`, `mlp`, the norms, `shared_experts`), so it is visited before the list gets polluted, which is why this is easy to miss. With `num_layers_per_pipeline_stage > 1` the stage is an `NNXSequentialPipelineStage` with children `layers_0`, `layers_1`, ...; `layers_0`'s non-MoE leaves are then visited before `layers_1`'s `MoeBlock_0`, and the routed-expert weights of every sub-layer after the first lose their `expert` axis in the BSW partition specs. Reproduction at the `PartitionSpec` level, using a Mixtral-style layer:

```
num_layers_per_pipeline_stage=2
  layers_0 MoeBlock_0/wi_0 -> P('expert', None, 'tensor')
  layers_1 MoeBlock_0/wi_0 -> P(None, None, 'tensor')   # expected P('expert', None, 'tensor')
```

**The fix.** Build a new list (`[*axes_to_remove, "expert"]`) instead of appending to the argument. Results are unchanged for single-layer stages and for non-MoE models; only the multiple-sub-layers-per-stage MoE case changes.

I have only reproduced this at the spec level. I have not run a multi-layer-per-stage MoE pipeline on TPU/GPU, so I can't quantify the runtime effect (I'd expect extra gathering and memory for the expert weights).

**Tests.** `pipeline_utils.py` had no direct unit tests. `tests/unit/pipeline_utils_test.py` (CPU only, `cpu_only` marker) covers:
- the partition-spec helpers (`get_mesh_axis_dim_indices`, `remove_gathered_mesh_axes`, `derive_stage_weight_partition_specs`, `strip_pipeline_repeat_logical_axis`, `is_spec_leaf`), including regression cases for the bug above;
- `is_static_param`, `flatten_nnx_state` / `unflatten_nnx_state`, `advance_rng_state`, the Linen-collection helpers and `PipelineContext`;
- `create_gradient_accumulation_scan`: outputs and gradients (eager and under `jit`) match a plain `jax.lax.scan` over the same step, including the accumulated `bsw` cotangent.

# Tests

```
python -m pytest tests/unit/pipeline_utils_test.py
```

- 44 tests pass on CPU (jax 0.11.1, flax 0.12.9, Python 3.12).
- With only the `pipeline_utils.py` change reverted, 5 failures appear (subtests counted separately): the `non_moe_block` case of `RemoveGatheredMeshAxesTest.test_does_not_modify_axes_to_remove`, `DeriveStageWeightPartitionSpecsTest.test_does_not_modify_axes_to_remove`, the `layers_1` and `layers_2` subtests of `test_moe_block_keeps_expert_axis_in_every_sublayer_of_a_stage`, and `test_moe_result_does_not_depend_on_sibling_traversal_order_sibling_sorts_before`. The rest pass either way.
- `pyink` (indentation 2, line length 122), `pylint` (flags from `.pre-commit-config.yaml`) and `codespell` are clean on both files.
- Not run: `tests/integration/pipeline_parallelism_test.py` and any TPU/GPU workload (they need the full dependency stack and accelerators).

title: fix(mhc test): let the batch scale with the device count
body:
# Description

`_setup_mhc` uses `per_device_batch_size` as the *global* batch of `self.x`, which is why it defaults to `jax.device_count()`. Three tests override it to 1, so on any host with more than one device the batch is smaller than the mesh: the FSDP axis tries to partition axis 0 four ways on a 4-device host and the layer fails with `IndivisibleError: array axis 0 is partitioned 4 times, but the dimension size is 1`.

They pass in CI only because the job that runs them (`cpu-unit`) has a single device. These tests are auto-marked `cpu_only`, so the 4-GPU `gpu-unit` job deselects them. Dropping the override and taking the helper's default keeps single-device behavior identical while making the batch divide the mesh anywhere else. Batch size is irrelevant to what these tests assert (kernel dispatch and block-size plumbing).

# Tests

Reproduce the failure on `main` and the fix on this branch with:

    XLA_FLAGS=--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=4 python -m pytest \
      tests/unit/mhc_test.py -k use_mhc_pallas_kernel

Verified on 4x AMD Instinct MI355X (ROCm 10, jax 0.11.1): the three tests fail on `main` with the
`IndivisibleError` above and pass on this branch. The full `tests/unit/mhc_test.py` file also passes there

title: fix(attention test): give the mask tests the axis rules the cp gate reads
body:
# Description

Three mask tests build a 2- or 4-device context mesh and assert the mask is derived from the load-balanced `segment_positions`. That path is guarded by `_load_balanced_context_parallel()`, which sizes cp by resolving
`activation_q_length` against the *ambient* flax rules - deliberately, so that eval running under `logical_axis_rules_for_eval` cannot claim a DUAL_CHUNK_SWAP order the input pipeline never applied.

The tests never enter an `axis_rules` context, so the logical name resolves to `P(None)`, `cp_size` comes out as 1, load balancing is skipped, and the op returns a plain index-order causal mask while the tests still expect the position-aware one. This makes the `activation_q_length` rule ambient around the op, the way the rest of the suite does, and sets `ulysses_context_sharding`, which the cp-size computation reads once the query axis actually resolves.

In the two `LoadBalancedMaskTest` cases only that one rule is made ambient rather than the whole stub config: those configs also declare `segment_ids_batch -> context`, which was inert while nothing made it ambient, and cannot hold here because `generate_attention_mask` would shard their batch-1 segment ids across the 4-way context mesh.

These tests skip unless 2+ devices are visible, and they are auto-marked `cpu_only` so the 4-GPU `gpu-unit` job deselects them - which is why CI has not been executing them at all.

# Tests

Reproduce the failure on `main` and the fix on this branch with:

    XLA_FLAGS=--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=4 python -m pytest \
      tests/unit/attention_test.py -k "uses_original_load_balanced_positions or uses_segment_positions"

Verified on 4x AMD Instinct MI355X (ROCm 10, jax 0.11.1): the three tests fail on `main` (plain causal mask,
then an `IndivisibleError` once the rule resolves) and pass on this branch. The full `tests/unit/attention_test.py`

title: MoE: zero-initialize the ragged all-to-all combine buffer when ragged_buffer_factor > 0
body:
# Description

Since [#4397](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/4397), `ragged_buffer_factor > 0` truncates overflow but combine all-to-all writes the truncated sizes at the original offsets, leaving unwritten interior rows in a `lax.empty` buffer. Weighted combine reads those rows at full router weight, introducing uninitialized values into activations and gradients on TPU/GPU; `lax.empty` reads as zero on CPU, hiding the bug from CPU CI. This breaks [#3541](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/3541)'s invariant that every `lax.empty` row is overwritten.

The combine buffer is now zero-initialized only when truncation is enabled; the default `ragged_buffer_factor=-1` path remains byte-identical. Dispatch still uses `lax.empty` because receives form a packed prefix and unwritten rows are never read.

# Tests

Added two CPU tests: one checks the emitted allocation primitive (`zeros` vs `empty`, since `empty` reads as zero on CPU), and one replays combine row copies to verify a dropped row reads zero. End-to-end: ran 24 DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B LoRA training steps on v6e-128 with `ragged_buffer_factor=1.015625` and smooth monotonic loss. Setup: `ici_expert_parallelism=16`, `ici_tensor_parallelism=8`, `ici_fsdp_parallelism=1`, `max_target_length=16384`, `per_device_batch_size=0.125` (global batch 16), `LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS=--xla_tpu_scoped_vmem_limit_kib=98304`, dynamic-splash attention path enabled.

- `pytest tests/unit/moe_test.py` — 22 passed, 38 skipped (`origin/main`: 20 passed; this PR adds 2).
- `pyink --check --pyink-indentation=2 --line-length=122 src/maxtext/layers/moe.py tests/unit/moe_test.py` — passed.
- Mutation check: forcing the combine allocation back to `lax.empty` fails the emitted-primitive regression test.

title: Weight router replay targets by the shifted mask
body:
# Description

`router_replay_gen_model_input_fn` builds `targets` as `jnp.roll(token_ids, -1, axis=-1)`, so position *i* predicts token *i+1*. `targets_segmentation` is the per-position loss weight, so the weight at *i* must be the mask of that **target** — `token_mask` shifted left by one. It was applied unshifted.

In `src/maxtext/training_engine/maxtext_engine.py`:

```python
-targets_segmentation = token_mask.at[:, -1].set(0)
+targets_segmentation = jnp.roll(token_mask, -1, axis=-1)
+targets_segmentation = targets_segmentation.at[:, -1].set(0)
```

**The effect.** On the packed path `token_mask` is the *action* mask: zero over each segment's prompt, one over its completion. A segment's last prompt slot is the position that predicts its first completion token, and unshifted it carries the prompt's `0`. That token is therefore never scored, and the segment trains on completion tokens 2..N. For a two-segment row with `token_mask = [0,1,1,0,1,1]` and `segment_ids = [1,1,1,2,2,2]`:

| | weights |
| --- | --- |
| before | `[0,1,0,0,1,0]` |
| after | `[1,1,0,1,1,0]` |

Each segment scored one completion token where it should have scored two. The loss is finite and the curve is plausible either way; the gradient is computed against a strict subset of the completion.

**The line predates its exposure.** `fe02583f2` (#4826) wrote it against `RouterReplayTrainerPayload`, whose caller supplied a whole-row mask — for which the shift changes only the wrap position, which the next line already zeroes. #5198 rewired the function to `RLTrainerPayload`, whose packed form supplies an action mask by construction. `git blame` points at #4826; the behaviour change is #5198's.

**The `same_segment` guard is retained**, and the shift does not subsume it. It zeroes each segment's last slot, where `roll` would otherwise make the *next* sequence's first token a target. Both are needed: the shift fixes the segment's leading edge, the guard its trailing edge.

**One case is left as a TODO.** On the padded (unpacked) path `token_mask` is `prompt_mask ++ completion_mask`, so it spans the prompt and the prompt is scored. That is unchanged by this PR in either direction. Whether router replay intends to score prompt tokens is undocumented, so it is marked rather than changed.

# Tests

`test_packed_action_mask_scores_each_segments_first_completion_token` in `tests/post_training/unit/router_replay_engine_test.py`. It fails on the parent commit and passes here.

**Why no existing test caught this.** When the payload carries no `segment_ids` the function falls back to `segment_ids = token_mask`, which makes every mask boundary coincide with a segment boundary — and there the shifted and unshifted forms are indistinguishable. Exposing the difference requires `segment_ids` **and** a mask with interior zeros, which no fixture supplied. The new test supplies both, and asserts the same expected weights for an action mask and for a full-completion mask, so it also pins the boundary handling the guard is responsible for.

100 tests and 6 subtests pass on CPU in ~167 s:

```
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu python -m pytest \
  tests/post_training/unit/router_replay_engine_test.py \
  tests/post_training/unit/maxtext_engine_test.py \
  tests/post_training/unit/tunix_adapter_test.py \
  tests/post_training/unit/maxtext_engine_packing_test.py
```

No TPU run. This changes which positions carry loss weight, not the shapes or the composition of the packed step, and the gradient-equivalence axes reported in #5198 use a full mask on both arms, so they do not discriminate between the two forms.

title: Fix pylint E1121 false positive on lru_cache cache_info in lora_utils_test
body:
# Description

Fixes the `Code Quality Check / Pre-commit Linters` failure on `main`, which is currently
blocking CI for any PR that touches (or rebases past) `tests/post_training/unit/lora_utils_test.py`.

The `pylint` hook fails with:

```
************* Module lora_utils_test
tests/post_training/unit/lora_utils_test.py:234:17: E1121: Too many positional arguments for function call (too-many-function-args)
```

This is a known `astroid` false positive. For a function decorated with `@lru_cache`, `astroid`
models the attached `cache_info` as a *bound* method that proxies the wrapped function. Because
`_load_lora_module_configs()` takes zero arguments, the implicit `self` looks like one positional
argument too many. (`cache_clear()` is modeled differently, which is why only `cache_info()` trips
the check.)

The fix is a narrowly scoped inline `# pylint: disable=too-many-function-args` on that single line,
plus a comment explaining why it is needed. The test's behavior and assertions are unchanged.
`useless-suppression` is disabled in `pylintrc`, so the suppression is safe even in environments
where `astroid` does not misfire.

# Tests

- Verified the exact failure in CI logs for the `Pre-commit Linters` job on `main`
  (run `35264142732`, job `105346958467`): `pylint` reported this single `E1121` error and all other
  hooks passed.
- The change is comment-only from a runtime perspective; `tests/post_training/unit/lora_utils_test.py`
  is unaffected functionally and `test_load_lora_module_configs_caching` still asserts
  `cache_info().hits` and `cache_info().currsize`.
- Confirmed the file still compiles (`python3 -m py_compile`) and the longest line is 108 characters,
  within the `pyink` (122) and `pylint` (125) limits, so the formatting hooks stay clean.

title: Plumb tunix gc_collect_after_weight_sync into the RL trainer
body:
## What

tunix exposes `ClusterConfig.gc_collect_after_weight_sync` (skip the full host `gc.collect()` after every weight sync). It cannot be set from a MaxText RL config, so the RL trainer always runs the per-step collection.

Adds the `RLConfig` field (default equals tunix's default, so existing configs are unchanged) and forwards it to the tunix `ClusterConfig`, filtered through `_kwargs_supported_by`: kwargs the installed tunix's constructor does not accept (checked via `inspect.signature`) are dropped with a log line instead of failing, so the pinned tunix (`post_train_github_deps.txt`, a8d70582, which predates the field) keeps working; once the pin is bumped the setting takes effect without further changes.

Also logs the resolved `GrpoConfig` on the standard (non-agentic) path, matching the agentic path, so the applied knob values are visible in the logs.

*Split out of the original two-knob version of this PR per review: the `reward_num_workers` half needs a picklable reward-fn wrapper to actually take effect (the current closure makes tunix's reward pool fall back to serial with a `PicklingError`), and follows in its own PR.*

## Effect

On a Qwen3-0.6B GRPO run the gc knob was worth ~1.2 s per step.

## Tests

`tests/post_training/unit/train_rl_test.py`: the new field defaults to tunix's default and accepts overrides (also declared in `configs/post_train/rl.yml`); `_kwargs_supported_by` additionally passes everything through for classes taking `**kwargs` or with no inspectable signature; `_kwargs_supported_by` keeps accepted kwargs (dataclass or plain class), drops unknown ones with a log line, and stays silent when nothing is dropped.

```
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest tests/post_training/unit/train_rl_test.py -k "tunix_knob or kwargs_supported"
```

title: [NNX] Remove Linen module code, dead code, and shared-primitive imports
body:
# Description

Continues the Delete-Linen effort: removes the last first-party Flax Linen *module* code, sweeps out dead Linen functions, and moves shared SPMD/init primitives off the `flax.linen` namespace onto their canonical `flax.core.spmd` / `jax.nn` homes. No behavior change — this is dead-code and duplicate removal plus namespace-only swaps. Validated locally on a TPU v6e-8 (cpu platform): 3530 unit tests collect with zero import errors, and the affected suites pass (`maxtext_utils_test` 106, `model_creation_utils_test` 38, `nnx_decoders_test` 53, `linears_test` 13, `tiling_test` 1).

Module / dead-code removal:
- Delete the unused `pipeline_deprecated.py` (a Linen `Pipeline`) and `decoders.py` (a 46-line vestige whose only symbol, `deepstack_process`, is a byte-identical duplicate of the copy in `nnx_decoders.py`; the one importer is repointed there).
- Drop a stray `@nn.compact` left on `MixtralDecoderLayer.__init__` (the class is an `nnx.Module`, so it was a no-op conversion leftover) and mixtral's now-unused linen import.
- Delete grep-confirmed zero-caller Linen functions: `create_nnx_sharded_model_hybrid`, `get_logical_annotations`, the Linen `get_prefill_kv_cache_annotations` / `get_kv_cache_annotations`, `vocab_tiling_linen_loss`, `create_flax_pipeline_scan` / `create_pipeline_stage` / `execute_pipeline_stage_flax`, `remove_logically_partition`, `kv_cache_as_linen` / `mla_kv_cache_as_linen`, `gpt3_layer_norm`, and the Linen `grpo_loss_fn`. The public GRPO `train_step` / `eval_step` already dispatch unconditionally to the `_nnx` variants, so `grpo_loss_fn` had no call sites; its algorithm docstring was folded into `grpo_loss_fn_nnx`.

Drop `flax.linen` from files that no longer need it. Where a file used `flax.linen` only for shared primitives whose values are the same objects on their canonical homes, move to those homes and remove the import (net −27 `flax.linen` import lines):
- `nn_partitioning.axis_rules` / `nn.logical_axis_rules` → `flax.core.spmd.logical_axis_rules` across the trainers, inference, and utils that used it. In the two files where a local parameter is also named `logical_axis_rules`, the import is aliased as `axis_rules` to avoid shadowing.

title: Refactor LoRA resharding, modernize NNX variable access, and streamline graph traversal
body:
# Description

Refactors the LoRA mesh sharding, modernizes Flax NNX variable access, streamlines model graph traversal, and improves checkpoint restore robustness in `lora_utils.py`:

1. **Targeted In-Place LoRA Resharding (`apply_lora_to_model`)**: Replaces full-model `nnx.split`/`nnx.merge` and `logical_to_mesh_sharding` with direct, in-place resharding of `nnx.LoRAParam` instances via `jax.make_array_from_callback`. This ensures LoRA parameters are replicated across the device mesh (DDP) while frozen base weights (and `QArray` quantized weights in QLoRA) retain their original FSDP/TP sharding on device HBM, avoiding device-placement mismatches and graph recreation overhead on multi-host topologies.
2. **Streamlined Model Traversal & Caching**: Consolidates 4 separate full-graph iterations in `apply_lora_to_model` (`qwix_rngs` deletion, resharding, LoRA enablement check, submodule verification) into a single pass, and adds `@lru_cache` to `_load_lora_module_configs()`.
3. **Flax NNX Variable Modernization**: Replaces deprecated `.value` getter and setter accesses with `.get_value()`, `.set_value()`, and `.set_metadata(...)` across `lora_utils.py`.
4. **Checkpoint Restore Robustness (`restore_lora_from_path`)**: Ensures that target parameter shardings are correctly coerced into `NamedSharding(mesh, pspec)` before `jax.device_put`, and verifies that restored leaves are materialized arrays (raising an informative `ValueError` rather than leaving silent `ShapeDtypeStruct`s).
5. **Hardened Adapter Path Resolution (`load_adapter`)**: Supports both GCS paths (`gs://...`) and local filesystem directories with standard `commit_success.txt` validation.

- Unit tests across all LoRA and SFT test suites passed (40/40):

title: Resolve step timing misattribution and isolate checkpoint overhead in MaxText.
body:
Resolve step timing misattribution and isolate checkpoint overhead in MaxText.

Previously, MaxText measured training step times using host-side wall-clock intervals between loop iterations (`now() - last_step_completion`). Because JAX dispatches steps asynchronously and the metric logger flushes metrics buffered from step N-1, this logic was broken in several ways:

1. Inaccurate Step 0 Time: The reported time for step 0 was artificially low because it only measured the asynchronous dispatch time.
2. Attribution Shift: Measuring `now() - last_step_completion` effectively measured the time taken for step N-1 to complete, but attributed it to step N+1.
3. Missing Overheads: Checkpointing, HLO dumps, eval, and profiling times were not included in the step time calculations. 
4. Broken Checkpoint Logs: Checkpointing acts as a synchronization barrier for step N. Because checkpointing blocked the host to perform D2H tensor transfers before the flush, it broke the logs around checkpoint boundaries, causing subsequent steps to enqueue instantly and artificially stall later.

We fix this by measuring the interval between log flushes, where the loss is actually synchronized:

- Eager Loss Synchronization before Step Time calculation: We force host-device synchronization on the main thread by converting the loss JAX array to a float inside `_flush_one_buffered_entry`. The step time is now calculated as the duration between consecutive eager loss synchronizations. Note that this synchronization was already occurring subsequently during final metrics serialization; moving it forward simply establishes a clean boundary to accurately measure step times.
- Loop Reordering: `buffer_and_write_metrics` is moved before `maybe_save_checkpoint`. This ensures that metrics for step N-1 are flushed before step N's checkpointing sync barrier blocks the host thread.
- Timer Cleanup: Inaccurate host-loop timing variables (`last_step_completion` and `step_time_delta`) are removed.

This guarantees that all physical blocking copy overhead and host CPU serialization contention are accurately captured and cleanly attributed to the correct steps, eliminating the anomalies around step 0 and checkpoint boundaries.

title: feat: add moe_spread_experts_over_fsdp to enable spreading MoE experts over FSDP axis
body:
## Description

This PR adds support for spreading MoE expert weights over both the `expert` and `fsdp` mesh axes, enabling better memory efficiency when combining Mixture of Experts (MoE) with FSDP parallelism.

### Problem Solved

Under base rules, running an MoE model with FSDP > 1 either:
1. Replicates the expert stack across FSDP shards (embed-dim sharding only, OOM at scale), or
2. Collides logical axes that both resolve to the fsdp mesh axis (duplicate-axis sharding error)

### Solution

Spreads the expert dimension over [expert, fsdp] and releases the MoE embed dimension from fsdp so no tensor claims the same mesh axis twice. Unlike `shard_exp_on_fsdp` (which requires `ici_expert_parallelism = ici_tensor_parallelism = 1`), this composes with expert/tensor parallelism.

### Implementation Details

The feature provides three modes controlled by `moe_spread_experts_over_fsdp`:

- **'never'** (default): Keep base rules, preserves existing behavior
- **'auto'**: Apply when `num_experts` is divisible by `(ici_expert_parallelism * ici_fsdp_parallelism)`
- **'always'**: Apply and fail loudly if divisibility requirement not met

The implementation:
- Adds validation for divisibility checks
- Handles auto-fill case (fsdp == -1) by declining in 'auto' mode, proceeding in 'always' mode
- Transforms logical_axis_rules dynamically during config initialization
- Includes proper logging for debugging

### Changes

1. **src/maxtext/configs/base.yml** - Added `moe_spread_experts_over_fsdp` config parameter with documentation
2. **src/maxtext/configs/types.py** - Added `moe_spread_experts_over_fsdp` field to `MoEGeneral` pydantic model
3. **src/maxtext/configs/pyconfig.py** - Implemented `_maybe_spread_moe_experts_over_fsdp()` function with full validation logic
4. **tests/unit/pyconfig_test.py** - Added 14 comprehensive unit tests

## Tests

Comprehensive test coverage includes:

- ✓ All three modes ('never', 'auto', 'always')
- ✓ Divisibility validation (pass and fail cases)
- ✓ Auto-fill FSDP handling (-1 case)
- ✓ Edge cases (non-MoE models, trivial FSDP axis)
- ✓ Invalid mode error handling
- ✓ Both tuple and string axis format support

All syntax validated (Python and YAML). Tests can be run with:
```bash
python -m pytest tests/unit/pyconfig_test.py::PyconfigTest -k "moe_spread" -v
```

title: Add StreamIndex Kernel for CSA [Deepseek v4]
body:
# Description

Adds a fused Pallas TPU kernel (`csa_streamindex_score`) for DeepSeek-V4 Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) indexer scoring (for the forward pass)
BUGS: b/552514390

### Summary
- Fuses the $Q \cdot K^T$ matmul, ReLU, head weighting, and causal masking into on-chip VMEM to avoid materializing large intermediate tensors in HBM.
- Supports head-major layout $[B, H, S, D]$ and wraps with `@jax.custom_vjp`.
- Gated behind `use_csa_streamindex_kernel: bool = False` in `base.yml` with automatic fallback to standard einsum.
- Wrapped with `@jax.custom_vjp`: executes the fused Pallas kernel on the forward pass, and falls back to reference einsum autodiff (chunked) on the backward pass.

### Implementation
Tiles query tokens in blocks of 128 and compressed keys in blocks of 1024. For each block, it computes `relu(q @ k.T) * weights`, sums across all 64 heads directly in VMEM, applies the causal mask, and writes out the final `[B, S, W]` scores. This avoids allocating the 4D `[B, H, S, W]` scores tensor in HBM entirely.  It does **not include** the top-k at the end in-kernel.

# Tests

- Unit tests in [`tests/unit/csa_streamindex_test.py`](file:///usr/local/google/home/octatrifan/repos/maxtext/tests/unit/csa_streamindex_test.py):
  - Numerical parity vs reference einsum (with and without causal mask).
  - Custom VJP gradient parity.
  - Layer integration and fallback checks.
  - JAXPR graph verification (`pallas_call` vs `dot_general`).

Reproduce:
```bash
pytest tests/unit/csa_streamindex_test.py
```

# Performance
Microbenchmarks on a single TPU, just for the Index Scoring part (not e2e results). Compared against both the unchunked baseline einsum and the orthogonal head-chunking scan proposed in PR #5116 (which is a pure JAX solution to the OOM problem, but which requires more memory and is slower than StreamIndex)

StreamIndex Pallas Kernel vs. Head Chunking (PR #5116) vs. Baseline
Tested on single-chip TPU v5p. $H=64, D=128, W=S/4$:
| Sequence Length ($S$) | Batch ($B$) | Total Tokens | Baseline Einsum | Head Chunking (PR #5116, $c=16$) | StreamIndex Kernel | Kernel Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16,384 | 2 | 32,768 | 16.31 ms | 8.45 ms | **5.06 ms** | **1.67x vs PR / 3.22x vs Base** |
| 32,768 | 2 | 65,536 | 64.01 ms | 32.02 ms | **19.77 ms** | **1.62x vs PR / 3.24x vs Base** |
| 65,536 | 2 | 131,072 | OOM (274 GB req) | 125.90 ms (20.09 GiB) | **78.42 ms (18.04 GiB)** | **1.61x vs PR** |
| 65,536 | 4 | 262,144 | OOM | 251.84 ms (40.17 GiB) | **156.84 ms (36.08 GiB)** | **1.61x vs PR** |
| 65,536 | 8 | 524,288 | OOM | OOM | 313.53 ms (72.16 GiB) | **StreamIndex Only** |
| 131,072 | 1 | 131,072 | OOM | 247.27 ms (36.09 GiB) | **156.59 ms (34.04 GiB)** | **1.58x vs PR** |
| 131,072 | 2 | 262,144 | OOM | OOM| **313.14 ms (68.08 GiB)** | **StreamIndex Only** |
| 131,072 | 4 | 524,288 | OOM | OOM | OOM | Physical Limit (>96 GB) |
---
* **Speed**: StreamIndex is **1.6x faster** than Head Chunking and **3.2x faster** than baseline einsum across all context lengths.
* **Scalability**: StreamIndex supports **2x larger contexts** on a single TPU v5p, successfully running at $S=65\text{k}, B=8$ and $S=131\text{k}, B=2$ where Head chunking crashes with OOM.
* **Peak Memory**: StreamIndex uses less HBM by keeping intermediate score tensors on-chip in VMEM rather than HBM.

title: Skip HCA flash vs dot_product gradient parity test on TPU7x
body:
## What

`CompressedAttentionTest::test_hca_flash_vs_dot_product_unaligned_grads` fails on v7x only. This skips it there via the existing `skip_on_tpu7x` marker, with a `TODO(b/562604480)` to re-enable once the kernel is fixed.

## Why not just loosen the tolerance

The v7x mismatch is not benign drift. The test asserts `rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-6`, and CI reports 1131 mismatched elements with a max absolute difference of `2.16e-6`.

Reproducing the same config on v6e-8:

| grad wrt input (unpacked S=489) | v6e-8 | v7x (CI) |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| `max abs(grad_dot)` | 2.18e-06 | same config |
| `max abs(grad_flash - grad_dot)` | 7.36e-09 | 2.16e-06 |
| violations @ `rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-6` | 0 | 1131 |

Two things follow:

- Numpy's reported max *relative* difference among violations is only 3.37, so every violating element has `|ref| >= 2.16e-6 / 3.37 ~ 6.4e-7`. The disagreement is on the **largest-magnitude** gradient entries, not near-zero noise.
- On v6e, the entries with `|grad| > 1e-6` sit entirely at sequence positions 0-14 (the earliest keys, whose dK/dV accumulate across every later query block), and they agree to 6.1e-03 relative there.

Since `max |grad|` is only `2.18e-06`, absorbing a `2.16e-06` difference would require `atol ~ max|grad|`, which makes the assertion vacuous. Skipping on the affected platform keeps the check strict everywhere else, matching what `moe_test.py::test_gmm_grad_equivalence` already does for TPU7x.

The forward pass agrees on both platforms, so this looks like splash-backward accumulation precision on TPU7x rather than a masking/logic difference.

## Coverage retained on v7x

`test_compressed_attention_flash_vs_dot_product[hca_ratio128]`, `test_hca_flash_vs_dot_product_packed_crossing_window`, and `test_packed_vs_unpacked_equivalence[hca_flash]` still run and cover flash-vs-dot forward parity.

## Also

title: Add profiling to training engine
body:
# Description

This PR introduces step-driven profiling to the MaxText training engine to enable detailed performance tracing using JAX's profiling tools.

Specifically, this change:
- **Introduces a new `Profiler` class** (`src/maxtext/training_engine/profiler.py`) that manages the opening and closing of a profiling window based on the training configuration. 
- **Adds a `@_profiled_step` decorator** in `maxtext_engine.py` to automatically wrap execution steps (such as `fwd_bwd` and `update`) with `jax.profiler.StepTraceAnnotation`. This ensures regions are properly tagged with their `step_num` in the trace viewer.
- **Automatically drives the profiler** by activating it on the first call of an opened profile and deactivating it on the closing step.
- Ensures that any active profile is safely stopped if the engine shuts down unexpectedly via `engine.close()`.

# Tests

title: Make extract_answer linear in the response length
body:
## What

`extract_answer` finds the last `\boxed{...}` with a brace-balanced scan that slices `content[:op]` on every closing brace, i.e. O(len x braces) per completion. On long chain-of-thought completions that was about 1.5 s of every reward phase for a batch of 2048 (measured with per-function timers on a Qwen3-0.6B GRPO run).

This PR keeps the same single-pass stack scan but replaces the `content[:op].endswith(...)` slice with an O(1) `content.startswith("\\boxed", op - 6)` check, so the scan is linear in the response length in every case (20k unclosed or nested boxes: under 60 ms). This is an unconditional change to `extract_answer`; semantics are unchanged: the match that closes last wins and boxes that never close are ignored, and the regex / answer-tag fallbacks are untouched.

## Tests

`tests/post_training/unit/extract_answer_test.py`: two new cases (nested boxes, unclosed box) plus a 5000-case fuzz test against the previous stack-based implementation over an alphabet of braces, `\boxed{` and LaTeX fragments.

```
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest tests/post_training/unit/extract_answer_test.py
```

title: fix(config): allow warm start from load_parameters_path without checkpointing
body:
### Summary

`enable_checkpointing` gates the `CheckpointManager`, but the config validator also required it for `load_parameters_path`:

```python
if (self.load_parameters_path or self.load_full_state_path) and not self.enable_checkpointing:
    raise ValueError("You must set enable_checkpointing=True to load a checkpoint.")
```

Those are separate concerns. `load_parameters_path` is restored by its **own** `ocp.Checkpointer` inside `model_creation_utils.from_pretrained`, before the `CheckpointManager` is ever built:

https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/blob/main/src/maxtext/utils/model_creation_utils.py#L989-L997

It reads neither `enable_checkpointing` nor `checkpoint_dir`. The requirement was never real for that path. `load_full_state_path` is different — that one genuinely resumes through the manager (`train_utils.py:85-91`), so it keeps the check.

### Why this matters

The overly broad check meant **"warm start from these weights, but never write a checkpoint" could not be expressed**:

| intent | restore? | save? | expressible before? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enable_checkpointing=True` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `enable_checkpointing=False` | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| warm start, never save | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |

Callers wanting the third row had to set `enable_checkpointing=True` with an astronomically large `checkpoint_period`, and then separately suppress the two force-saves that bypass the period policy:

- `update()` → `save_checkpoint(..., force=True)` on `_resumed_mid_step` (`maxtext_engine.py:1758-1763`)
- `close()` → `save_checkpoint(metadata=None, force=True)` (`maxtext_engine.py:2244-2246`)

Orbax's own `read_only=True` does not help here, because `save(force=True)` skips `should_save()`, which is where `read_only` is enforced (`checkpoint_manager.py:1447`).

### Why no engine change is needed

With `enable_checkpointing=False`, both force-save sites are **already** correctly gated by existing guards:

| site | existing guard | result |
|---|---|---|
| `update()` resumed-mid-step | `maxtext_engine.py:1854` — `if not enable_checkpointing ... return` | skipped |
| `close()` final save | `maxtext_engine.py:2244` — `if enable_checkpointing and ...` | skipped |

So narrowing the validator is sufficient on its own. No new config knob, no change to the engine.

### Changes

- `src/maxtext/configs/types.py` — narrow the validator to `load_full_state_path`.
- `src/maxtext/configs/pyconfig_deprecated.py` — narrow the mirrored legacy assertion so the two paths cannot disagree.
- `tests/unit/pyconfig_test.py` — three regression tests: warm start without checkpointing is allowed, full-state resume without checkpointing still raises, and the pre-existing warm-start-with-checkpointing combination still works.

### Compatibility

This only **relaxes** a restriction. Every configuration valid today stays valid and behaves identically; the sole behavioral change is that a previously-rejected combination now runs as a warm start without saving.

### Follow-up

Unblocks removing the corresponding workaround from Tunix, where it currently lives in `_MeshBoundTrainer` (a shim the Tunix team wants to delete).
